case_info.scenario: A 62-year-old female presented with a generalized vesiculobullous rash of 4 months’ duration. The rash was insidious in onset and pruritic in nature. It started over the lips and gradually progressed to involve the oral mucosa and skin of the whole body. The patient also reported dry cough, dysuria, and tenesmus for a similar duration. Skin biopsy was suggestive of Stevens-Johnson syndrome. Computed tomography scan performed for diagnostic evaluation showed a mass in the mesentery. Biopsy from the mass indicated follicular lymphoma.18F-fluorodeoxyglucose (18F-FDG) positron emission tomography–computed tomography (PET-CT) scan was next performed for the staging of lymphoma. Maximum intensity projection image (Figure 1A) showed heterogeneous uptake of18F-FDG in the skin of the visualized body. There was a distinctive visualization of almost the entire facial contour of the patient secondary to inflammation of the facial skin and the mucosa of the conjunctiva, nasal cavity, lips, and oral cavity (Figure 1B).18F-FDG uptake was also noticed along the mucosa of the esophagus, stomach, and intestines. The mesenteric mass showed low-intensity18F-FDG uptake. The patient started taking corticosteroid and cyclophosphamide-based prephase chemotherapy due to poor general condition. The clinical course was complicated by lower respiratory tract infection, which progressed to septic shock and multiorgan dysfunction, and the patient died due to infective complications.
case_info.caption: Maximum intensity projection image (A) of18F-fluorodeoxyglucose (18F-FDG) positron emission tomography–computed tomography with heterogeneously scattered uptake of 18F-FDG in the skin. The dashed box in panel A highlights the facial features closely corresponding to the clinical photograph of the patient (B).
case_info.explanation: The most plausible diagnosis is paraneoplastic pemphigus (PNP). PNP can be a paraneoplastic manifestation of several different neoplastic disorders. However, hematolymphoid malignant neoplasms are the most frequently associated primary conditions in adults, and non-Hodgkin lymphoma is the most common.1The case presented was diagnosed with follicular lymphoma (Figure 2). The mucocutaneous manifestations of PNP are insidious in onset differentiating it from the more rapid onset expected in drug-induced Stevens-Johnson syndrome and the cutaneous variant of tumor lysis syndrome. Primary cutaneous involvement by lymphoma typically presents as a clinical spectrum ranging from patches or plaques to tumor stage accompanied by various systemic symptoms. PNP is an autoimmune condition, and there is a growing consensus that affliction of several other organ systems is not uncommon even though skin involvement is the most notable feature of this condition. Hence the termparaneoplastic multiorgan syndromehas been suggested as an alternative. The high mortality rate associated with the condition may more plausibly be explained by multiorgan dysfunction. Although it is more common for the underlying malignant neoplasm to be detected before PNP, the skin rash may precede the detection of malignant neoplasm, especially if the latter is of indolent nature (eg, low-grade lymphoma). Ohzono et al2reported in a series of 104 patients with PNP that 12 cases had no detectable tumor. Immune dysregulation, affecting both humoral and cell-mediated immunity, is hypothesized as the pathophysiological mechanism behind PNP. Overactive humoral immunity with the formation of autoantibodies to several epithelial antigens, primarily the desmoplakins and anchor proteins responsible for epidermal cell adhesion, is reported in such cases.3Presence of autoantibodies to periplakin and envoplakin is proposed as a specific laboratory marker.4The underlying malignant neoplasm may induce immune dysregulation through cross-reactivity of antibodies against tumor antigens and epithelial antigens.5Further, accumulation of cluster of differentiation 8+ T lymphocytes and natural killer cells have been reported at the dermal-epidermal junction in PNP cases.6 Besides polymorphic skin lesions, mucositis is characteristic of PNP. Oral mucosa is most frequently affected3and is the initial site of presentation in about 50% of patients,6as also in the presented case. Mucosal involvement of conjunctiva, nasopharynx, esophagus, gastrointestinal tract, and anogenital region may also be present.7Skin rash typically follows the manifestations of mucosal involvement and shows considerable variation in the type of lesions and extent of involvement. Papulosquamous, targetoid, or vesiculobullous lesions may occur in isolation, or 1 type may predominate the others in a mixed pattern. Extensive cutaneous desquamation similar to toxic epidermal necrolysis may also occur, as in the presented case.3,8Patients may develop involvement of respiratory epithelium with small airway predisposition leading to bronchiolitis. Immunological reactions targeting plakin proteins in small airway epithelium is the proposed mechanism.9Bronchiolitis obliterans is a late and possibly life-threatening complication. The presented case also highlights the role of whole-body imaging like18F-FDG PET-CT in evaluating cases presenting with similar clinical profiles and in narrowing down the differential diagnoses.18F-FDG PET-CT may accurately map the disease activity in paraneoplastic inflammatory skin conditions and localize the primary cancers. The treatment of the underlying neoplasm is not strongly associated with remission of PNP. Instead, the latter is more likely to have a progressive course despite control of the malignant neoplasm.10Systemic therapy with glucocorticoids, alone or in combination with other immunosuppressive agents like mycophenolate mofetil, azathioprine, rituximab, or intravenous immunoglobulin has been described to be effective, but the evidence is limited to case reports. The prognosis remains very poor.

   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.

   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a

case_info.explanation: The most plausible diagnosis is paraneoplastic pemphigus (PNP). PNP can be a paraneoplastic manifestation of several different neoplastic disorders. However, hematolymphoid malignant neoplasms are the most frequently associated primary conditions in adults, and non-Hodgkin lymphoma is the most common.1The case presented was diagnosed with follicular lymphoma (Figure 2). The mucocutaneous manifestations of PNP are insidious in onset differentiating it from the more rapid onset expected in drug-induced Stevens-Johnson syndrome and the cutaneous variant of tumor lysis syndrome. Primary cutaneous involvement by lymphoma typically presents as a clinical spectrum ranging from patches or plaques to tumor stage accompanied by various systemic symptoms. PNP is an autoimmune condition, and there is a growing consensus that affliction of several other organ systems is not uncommon even though skin involvement is the most notable feature of this condition. Hence the termparaneoplastic multiorgan syndromehas been suggested as an alternative. The high mortality rate associated with the condition may more plausibly be explained by multiorgan dysfunction. Although it is more common for the underlying malignant neoplasm to be detected before PNP, the skin rash may precede the detection of malignant neoplasm, especially if the latter is of indolent nature (eg, low-grade lymphoma). Ohzono et al2reported in a series of 104 patients with PNP that 12 cases had no detectable tumor. Immune dysregulation, affecting both humoral and cell-mediated immunity, is hypothesized as the pathophysiological mechanism behind PNP. Overactive humoral immunity with the formation of autoantibodies to several epithelial antigens, primarily the desmoplakins and anchor proteins responsible for epidermal cell adhesion, is reported in such cases.3Presence of autoantibodies to periplakin and envoplakin is proposed as a specific laboratory marker.4The underlying malignant neoplasm may induce immune dysregulation through cross-reactivity of antibodies against tumor antigens and epithelial antigens.5Further, accumulation of cluster of differentiation 8+ T lymphocytes and natural killer cells have been reported at the dermal-epidermal junction in PNP cases.6 Besides polymorphic skin lesions, mucositis is characteristic of PNP. Oral mucosa is most frequently affected3and is the initial site of presentation in about 50% of patients,6as also in the presented case. Mucosal involvement of conjunctiva, nasopharynx, esophagus, gastrointestinal tract, and anogenital region may also be present.7Skin rash typically follows the manifestations of mucosal involvement and shows considerable variation in the type of lesions and extent of involvement. Papulosquamous, targetoid, or vesiculobullous lesions may occur in isolation, or 1 type may predominate the others in a mixed pattern. Extensive cutaneous desquamation similar to toxic epidermal necrolysis may also occur, as in the presented case.3,8Patients may develop involvement of respiratory epithelium with small airway predisposition leading to bronchiolitis. Immunological reactions targeting plakin proteins in small airway epithelium is the proposed mechanism.9Bronchiolitis obliterans is a late and possibly life-threatening complication. The presented case also highlights the role of whole-body imaging like18F-FDG PET-CT in evaluating cases presenting with similar clinical profiles and in narrowing down the differential diagnoses.18F-FDG PET-CT may accurately map the disease activity in paraneoplastic inflammatory skin conditions and localize the primary cancers. The treatment of the underlying neoplasm is not strongly associated with remission of PNP. Instead, the latter is more likely to have a progressive course despite control of the malignant neoplasm.10Systemic therapy with glucocorticoids, alone or in combination with other immunosuppressive agents like mycophenolate mofetil, azathioprine, rituximab, or intravenous immunoglobulin has been described to be effective, but the evidence is limited to case reports. The prognosis remains very poor.

the best decision, at the lowest cognitive cost to the clinician. You control HOW the AI speaks,
never WHAT the medical answer is (that is the AI's job). Each turn you choose ONE control stage and
write a short guidance instruction for the AI's next utterance.

The 3 control stages (pick exactly one, and only from the reachable list you are given):

- EXPAND  — cheap, safe, broadens the picture. Elicit the clinician's reasoning, ask them to
            justify, or surface a missing goal/criterion/perspective. Do NOT yet evaluate or push
            an option. Effect is often delayed (sets up a later CHALLENGE). Use when the state is

            you have reason to think the clinician's current position is wrong or under-examined.

            or confirm an agreement already reached. This is the STOP / pacing lever — stop
            spending burden once belief has settled.

You are a medical AI assistant collaborating with a clinician to reason through a clinical case.
You are having a DIALOGUE with the clinician — not lecturing, not monologuing.

[Core Objective]
Help the clinician reach the correct diagnosis or management decision through structured deliberation.

[Interaction Guidelines]
1. **Collaboration**: Work as a partner. Build upon the clinician's correct reasoning.
2. **Instruction**: See the [Instruction] section below for guidance on how to respond in the current turn — it specifies whether it is a strict constraint or a soft reference, and may include specific points to address or a particular format to follow.
3. **Safety First**: Patient safety overrides politeness. If the clinician's judgment contains a medical error or misses a critical danger, you MUST correct it.
4. **Concise turns**: Each turn should be 2–4 sentences. Do not produce long lists or procedure walkthroughs.

[Case]
A 62-year-old female presented with a generalized vesiculobullous rash of 4 months’ duration. The rash was insidious in onset and pruritic in nature. It started over the lips and gradually progressed to involve the oral mucosa and skin of the whole body. The patient also reported dry cough, dysuria, and tenesmus for a similar duration. Skin biopsy was suggestive of Stevens-Johnson syndrome. Computed tomography scan performed for diagnostic evaluation showed a mass in the mesentery. Biopsy from the mass indicated follicular lymphoma.18F-fluorodeoxyglucose (18F-FDG) positron emission tomography–computed tomography (PET-CT) scan was next performed for the staging of lymphoma. Maximum intensity projection image (Figure 1A) showed heterogeneous uptake of18F-FDG in the skin of the visualized body. There was a distinctive visualization of almost the entire facial contour of the patient secondary to inflammation of the facial skin and the mucosa of the conjunctiva, nasal cavity, lips, and oral cavity (Figure 1B).18F-FDG uptake was also noticed along the mucosa of the esophagus, stomach, and intestines. The mesenteric mass showed low-intensity18F-FDG uptake. The patient started taking corticosteroid and cyclophosphamide-based prephase chemotherapy due to poor general condition. The clinical course was complicated by lower respiratory tract infection, which progressed to septic shock and multiorgan dysfunction, and the patient died due to infective complications.

[NASA-TLX-derived scoring dimensions]

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   Scoring:
   1 = Very low frustration; the message is calm, respectful, and unlikely to pressure you.
       Example: "That reasoning makes sense. One small point to keep in mind is X."
   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.
       Example: "I may be missing something, but could we double-check whether X fits
       the case?"
   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a
       somewhat pressuring way.
       Example: "I am concerned that this diagnosis may not explain the tachycardia.
       Could you justify why you still prefer it?"
   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.
       Example: "This seems like a serious oversight. You need to explain why you are
       dismissing PE."
   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.
       Example: "Your reasoning is clearly flawed, and proceeding with your diagnosis
       would be unsafe."
   Frustration is not just "the AI disagreed with me" -- it is about HOW the disagreement is
   delivered. A polite challenge ("One concern is that the current diagnosis may not fully
   explain the tachycardia. Could we check PE before finalizing?") should score low-to-mid
   even though it is a real challenge. An aggressive or repetitive one ("You still haven't
   justified why PE is ruled out. This is a serious oversight.") should score high.

It started over the lips and gradually progressed to involve the oral mucosa and skin of the whole body. The patient also reported dry cough, dysuria, and tenesmus for a similar duration. Skin biopsy was suggestive of Stevens-Johnson syndrome. Computed tomography scan performed for diagnostic evaluation showed a mass in the mesentery. Biopsy from the mass indicated follicular lymphoma.18F-fluorodeoxyglucose (18F-FDG) positron emission tomography–computed tomography (PET-CT) scan was next performed for the staging of lymphoma. Maximum intensity projection image (Figure 1A) showed heterogeneous uptake of18F-FDG in the skin of the visualized body. There was a distinctive visualization of almost the entire facial contour of the patient secondary to inflammation of the facial skin and the mucosa of the conjunctiva, nasal cavity, lips, and oral cavity (Figure 1B).18F-FDG uptake was also noticed along the mucosa of the esophagus, stomach, and intestines. The mesenteric mass showed low-intensity18F-FDG uptake. The patient started taking corticosteroid and cyclophosphamide-based prephase chemotherapy due to poor general condition. The clinical course was complicated by lower respiratory tract infection, which progressed to septic shock and multiorgan dysfunction, and the patient died due to infective complications.

  C. Paraneoplastic pemphigus

case_info.explanation: The most plausible diagnosis is paraneoplastic pemphigus (PNP). PNP can be a paraneoplastic manifestation of several different neoplastic disorders. However, hematolymphoid malignant neoplasms are the most frequently associated primary conditions in adults, and non-Hodgkin lymphoma is the most common.1The case presented was diagnosed with follicular lymphoma (Figure 2). The mucocutaneous manifestations of PNP are insidious in onset differentiating it from the more rapid onset expected in drug-induced Stevens-Johnson syndrome and the cutaneous variant of tumor lysis syndrome. Primary cutaneous involvement by lymphoma typically presents as a clinical spectrum ranging from patches or plaques to tumor stage accompanied by various systemic symptoms. PNP is an autoimmune condition, and there is a growing consensus that affliction of several other organ systems is not uncommon even though skin involvement is the most notable feature of this condition. Hence the termparaneoplastic multiorgan syndromehas been suggested as an alternative. The high mortality rate associated with the condition may more plausibly be explained by multiorgan dysfunction. Although it is more common for the underlying malignant neoplasm to be detected before PNP, the skin rash may precede the detection of malignant neoplasm, especially if the latter is of indolent nature (eg, low-grade lymphoma). Ohzono et al2reported in a series of 104 patients with PNP that 12 cases had no detectable tumor. Immune dysregulation, affecting both humoral and cell-mediated immunity, is hypothesized as the pathophysiological mechanism behind PNP. Overactive humoral immunity with the formation of autoantibodies to several epithelial antigens, primarily the desmoplakins and anchor proteins responsible for epidermal cell adhesion, is reported in such cases.3Presence of autoantibodies to periplakin and envoplakin is proposed as a specific laboratory marker.4The underlying malignant neoplasm may induce immune dysregulation through cross-reactivity of antibodies against tumor antigens and epithelial antigens.5Further, accumulation of cluster of differentiation 8+ T lymphocytes and natural killer cells have been reported at the dermal-epidermal junction in PNP cases.6 Besides polymorphic skin lesions, mucositis is characteristic of PNP. Oral mucosa is most frequently affected3and is the initial site of presentation in about 50% of patients,6as also in the presented case. Mucosal involvement of conjunctiva, nasopharynx, esophagus, gastrointestinal tract, and anogenital region may also be present.7Skin rash typically follows the manifestations of mucosal involvement and shows considerable variation in the type of lesions and extent of involvement. Papulosquamous, targetoid, or vesiculobullous lesions may occur in isolation, or 1 type may predominate the others in a mixed pattern. Extensive cutaneous desquamation similar to toxic epidermal necrolysis may also occur, as in the presented case.3,8Patients may develop involvement of respiratory epithelium with small airway predisposition leading to bronchiolitis. Immunological reactions targeting plakin proteins in small airway epithelium is the proposed mechanism.9Bronchiolitis obliterans is a late and possibly life-threatening complication. The presented case also highlights the role of whole-body imaging like18F-FDG PET-CT in evaluating cases presenting with similar clinical profiles and in narrowing down the differential diagnoses.18F-FDG PET-CT may accurately map the disease activity in paraneoplastic inflammatory skin conditions and localize the primary cancers. The treatment of the underlying neoplasm is not strongly associated with remission of PNP. Instead, the latter is more likely to have a progressive course despite control of the malignant neoplasm.10Systemic therapy with glucocorticoids, alone or in combination with other immunosuppressive agents like mycophenolate mofetil, azathioprine, rituximab, or intravenous immunoglobulin has been described to be effective, but the evidence is limited to case reports. The prognosis remains very poor.

case_info.explanation: The most plausible diagnosis is paraneoplastic pemphigus (PNP). PNP can be a paraneoplastic manifestation of several different neoplastic disorders. However, hematolymphoid malignant neoplasms are the most frequently associated primary conditions in adults, and non-Hodgkin lymphoma is the most common.1The case presented was diagnosed with follicular lymphoma (Figure 2). The mucocutaneous manifestations of PNP are insidious in onset differentiating it from the more rapid onset expected in drug-induced Stevens-Johnson syndrome and the cutaneous variant of tumor lysis syndrome. Primary cutaneous involvement by lymphoma typically presents as a clinical spectrum ranging from patches or plaques to tumor stage accompanied by various systemic symptoms. PNP is an autoimmune condition, and there is a growing consensus that affliction of several other organ systems is not uncommon even though skin involvement is the most notable feature of this condition. Hence the termparaneoplastic multiorgan syndromehas been suggested as an alternative. The high mortality rate associated with the condition may more plausibly be explained by multiorgan dysfunction. Although it is more common for the underlying malignant neoplasm to be detected before PNP, the skin rash may precede the detection of malignant neoplasm, especially if the latter is of indolent nature (eg, low-grade lymphoma). Ohzono et al2reported in a series of 104 patients with PNP that 12 cases had no detectable tumor. Immune dysregulation, affecting both humoral and cell-mediated immunity, is hypothesized as the pathophysiological mechanism behind PNP. Overactive humoral immunity with the formation of autoantibodies to several epithelial antigens, primarily the desmoplakins and anchor proteins responsible for epidermal cell adhesion, is reported in such cases.3Presence of autoantibodies to periplakin and envoplakin is proposed as a specific laboratory marker.4The underlying malignant neoplasm may induce immune dysregulation through cross-reactivity of antibodies against tumor antigens and epithelial antigens.5Further, accumulation of cluster of differentiation 8+ T lymphocytes and natural killer cells have been reported at the dermal-epidermal junction in PNP cases.6 Besides polymorphic skin lesions, mucositis is characteristic of PNP. Oral mucosa is most frequently affected3and is the initial site of presentation in about 50% of patients,6as also in the presented case. Mucosal involvement of conjunctiva, nasopharynx, esophagus, gastrointestinal tract, and anogenital region may also be present.7Skin rash typically follows the manifestations of mucosal involvement and shows considerable variation in the type of lesions and extent of involvement. Papulosquamous, targetoid, or vesiculobullous lesions may occur in isolation, or 1 type may predominate the others in a mixed pattern. Extensive cutaneous desquamation similar to toxic epidermal necrolysis may also occur, as in the presented case.3,8Patients may develop involvement of respiratory epithelium with small airway predisposition leading to bronchiolitis. Immunological reactions targeting plakin proteins in small airway epithelium is the proposed mechanism.9Bronchiolitis obliterans is a late and possibly life-threatening complication. The presented case also highlights the role of whole-body imaging like18F-FDG PET-CT in evaluating cases presenting with similar clinical profiles and in narrowing down the differential diagnoses.18F-FDG PET-CT may accurately map the disease activity in paraneoplastic inflammatory skin conditions and localize the primary cancers. The treatment of the underlying neoplasm is not strongly associated with remission of PNP. Instead, the latter is more likely to have a progressive course despite control of the malignant neoplasm.10Systemic therapy with glucocorticoids, alone or in combination with other immunosuppressive agents like mycophenolate mofetil, azathioprine, rituximab, or intravenous immunoglobulin has been described to be effective, but the evidence is limited to case reports. The prognosis remains very poor.

case_info.explanation: The most plausible diagnosis is paraneoplastic pemphigus (PNP). PNP can be a paraneoplastic manifestation of several different neoplastic disorders. However, hematolymphoid malignant neoplasms are the most frequently associated primary conditions in adults, and non-Hodgkin lymphoma is the most common.1The case presented was diagnosed with follicular lymphoma (Figure 2). The mucocutaneous manifestations of PNP are insidious in onset differentiating it from the more rapid onset expected in drug-induced Stevens-Johnson syndrome and the cutaneous variant of tumor lysis syndrome. Primary cutaneous involvement by lymphoma typically presents as a clinical spectrum ranging from patches or plaques to tumor stage accompanied by various systemic symptoms. PNP is an autoimmune condition, and there is a growing consensus that affliction of several other organ systems is not uncommon even though skin involvement is the most notable feature of this condition. Hence the termparaneoplastic multiorgan syndromehas been suggested as an alternative. The high mortality rate associated with the condition may more plausibly be explained by multiorgan dysfunction. Although it is more common for the underlying malignant neoplasm to be detected before PNP, the skin rash may precede the detection of malignant neoplasm, especially if the latter is of indolent nature (eg, low-grade lymphoma). Ohzono et al2reported in a series of 104 patients with PNP that 12 cases had no detectable tumor. Immune dysregulation, affecting both humoral and cell-mediated immunity, is hypothesized as the pathophysiological mechanism behind PNP. Overactive humoral immunity with the formation of autoantibodies to several epithelial antigens, primarily the desmoplakins and anchor proteins responsible for epidermal cell adhesion, is reported in such cases.3Presence of autoantibodies to periplakin and envoplakin is proposed as a specific laboratory marker.4The underlying malignant neoplasm may induce immune dysregulation through cross-reactivity of antibodies against tumor antigens and epithelial antigens.5Further, accumulation of cluster of differentiation 8+ T lymphocytes and natural killer cells have been reported at the dermal-epidermal junction in PNP cases.6 Besides polymorphic skin lesions, mucositis is characteristic of PNP. Oral mucosa is most frequently affected3and is the initial site of presentation in about 50% of patients,6as also in the presented case. Mucosal involvement of conjunctiva, nasopharynx, esophagus, gastrointestinal tract, and anogenital region may also be present.7Skin rash typically follows the manifestations of mucosal involvement and shows considerable variation in the type of lesions and extent of involvement. Papulosquamous, targetoid, or vesiculobullous lesions may occur in isolation, or 1 type may predominate the others in a mixed pattern. Extensive cutaneous desquamation similar to toxic epidermal necrolysis may also occur, as in the presented case.3,8Patients may develop involvement of respiratory epithelium with small airway predisposition leading to bronchiolitis. Immunological reactions targeting plakin proteins in small airway epithelium is the proposed mechanism.9Bronchiolitis obliterans is a late and possibly life-threatening complication. The presented case also highlights the role of whole-body imaging like18F-FDG PET-CT in evaluating cases presenting with similar clinical profiles and in narrowing down the differential diagnoses.18F-FDG PET-CT may accurately map the disease activity in paraneoplastic inflammatory skin conditions and localize the primary cancers. The treatment of the underlying neoplasm is not strongly associated with remission of PNP. Instead, the latter is more likely to have a progressive course despite control of the malignant neoplasm.10Systemic therapy with glucocorticoids, alone or in combination with other immunosuppressive agents like mycophenolate mofetil, azathioprine, rituximab, or intravenous immunoglobulin has been described to be effective, but the evidence is limited to case reports. The prognosis remains very poor.

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."

   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.

   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a

   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.

case_info.explanation: The most plausible diagnosis is paraneoplastic pemphigus (PNP). PNP can be a paraneoplastic manifestation of several different neoplastic disorders. However, hematolymphoid malignant neoplasms are the most frequently associated primary conditions in adults, and non-Hodgkin lymphoma is the most common.1The case presented was diagnosed with follicular lymphoma (Figure 2). The mucocutaneous manifestations of PNP are insidious in onset differentiating it from the more rapid onset expected in drug-induced Stevens-Johnson syndrome and the cutaneous variant of tumor lysis syndrome. Primary cutaneous involvement by lymphoma typically presents as a clinical spectrum ranging from patches or plaques to tumor stage accompanied by various systemic symptoms. PNP is an autoimmune condition, and there is a growing consensus that affliction of several other organ systems is not uncommon even though skin involvement is the most notable feature of this condition. Hence the termparaneoplastic multiorgan syndromehas been suggested as an alternative. The high mortality rate associated with the condition may more plausibly be explained by multiorgan dysfunction. Although it is more common for the underlying malignant neoplasm to be detected before PNP, the skin rash may precede the detection of malignant neoplasm, especially if the latter is of indolent nature (eg, low-grade lymphoma). Ohzono et al2reported in a series of 104 patients with PNP that 12 cases had no detectable tumor. Immune dysregulation, affecting both humoral and cell-mediated immunity, is hypothesized as the pathophysiological mechanism behind PNP. Overactive humoral immunity with the formation of autoantibodies to several epithelial antigens, primarily the desmoplakins and anchor proteins responsible for epidermal cell adhesion, is reported in such cases.3Presence of autoantibodies to periplakin and envoplakin is proposed as a specific laboratory marker.4The underlying malignant neoplasm may induce immune dysregulation through cross-reactivity of antibodies against tumor antigens and epithelial antigens.5Further, accumulation of cluster of differentiation 8+ T lymphocytes and natural killer cells have been reported at the dermal-epidermal junction in PNP cases.6 Besides polymorphic skin lesions, mucositis is characteristic of PNP. Oral mucosa is most frequently affected3and is the initial site of presentation in about 50% of patients,6as also in the presented case. Mucosal involvement of conjunctiva, nasopharynx, esophagus, gastrointestinal tract, and anogenital region may also be present.7Skin rash typically follows the manifestations of mucosal involvement and shows considerable variation in the type of lesions and extent of involvement. Papulosquamous, targetoid, or vesiculobullous lesions may occur in isolation, or 1 type may predominate the others in a mixed pattern. Extensive cutaneous desquamation similar to toxic epidermal necrolysis may also occur, as in the presented case.3,8Patients may develop involvement of respiratory epithelium with small airway predisposition leading to bronchiolitis. Immunological reactions targeting plakin proteins in small airway epithelium is the proposed mechanism.9Bronchiolitis obliterans is a late and possibly life-threatening complication. The presented case also highlights the role of whole-body imaging like18F-FDG PET-CT in evaluating cases presenting with similar clinical profiles and in narrowing down the differential diagnoses.18F-FDG PET-CT may accurately map the disease activity in paraneoplastic inflammatory skin conditions and localize the primary cancers. The treatment of the underlying neoplasm is not strongly associated with remission of PNP. Instead, the latter is more likely to have a progressive course despite control of the malignant neoplasm.10Systemic therapy with glucocorticoids, alone or in combination with other immunosuppressive agents like mycophenolate mofetil, azathioprine, rituximab, or intravenous immunoglobulin has been described to be effective, but the evidence is limited to case reports. The prognosis remains very poor.

case_info.explanation: The most plausible diagnosis is paraneoplastic pemphigus (PNP). PNP can be a paraneoplastic manifestation of several different neoplastic disorders. However, hematolymphoid malignant neoplasms are the most frequently associated primary conditions in adults, and non-Hodgkin lymphoma is the most common.1The case presented was diagnosed with follicular lymphoma (Figure 2). The mucocutaneous manifestations of PNP are insidious in onset differentiating it from the more rapid onset expected in drug-induced Stevens-Johnson syndrome and the cutaneous variant of tumor lysis syndrome. Primary cutaneous involvement by lymphoma typically presents as a clinical spectrum ranging from patches or plaques to tumor stage accompanied by various systemic symptoms. PNP is an autoimmune condition, and there is a growing consensus that affliction of several other organ systems is not uncommon even though skin involvement is the most notable feature of this condition. Hence the termparaneoplastic multiorgan syndromehas been suggested as an alternative. The high mortality rate associated with the condition may more plausibly be explained by multiorgan dysfunction. Although it is more common for the underlying malignant neoplasm to be detected before PNP, the skin rash may precede the detection of malignant neoplasm, especially if the latter is of indolent nature (eg, low-grade lymphoma). Ohzono et al2reported in a series of 104 patients with PNP that 12 cases had no detectable tumor. Immune dysregulation, affecting both humoral and cell-mediated immunity, is hypothesized as the pathophysiological mechanism behind PNP. Overactive humoral immunity with the formation of autoantibodies to several epithelial antigens, primarily the desmoplakins and anchor proteins responsible for epidermal cell adhesion, is reported in such cases.3Presence of autoantibodies to periplakin and envoplakin is proposed as a specific laboratory marker.4The underlying malignant neoplasm may induce immune dysregulation through cross-reactivity of antibodies against tumor antigens and epithelial antigens.5Further, accumulation of cluster of differentiation 8+ T lymphocytes and natural killer cells have been reported at the dermal-epidermal junction in PNP cases.6 Besides polymorphic skin lesions, mucositis is characteristic of PNP. Oral mucosa is most frequently affected3and is the initial site of presentation in about 50% of patients,6as also in the presented case. Mucosal involvement of conjunctiva, nasopharynx, esophagus, gastrointestinal tract, and anogenital region may also be present.7Skin rash typically follows the manifestations of mucosal involvement and shows considerable variation in the type of lesions and extent of involvement. Papulosquamous, targetoid, or vesiculobullous lesions may occur in isolation, or 1 type may predominate the others in a mixed pattern. Extensive cutaneous desquamation similar to toxic epidermal necrolysis may also occur, as in the presented case.3,8Patients may develop involvement of respiratory epithelium with small airway predisposition leading to bronchiolitis. Immunological reactions targeting plakin proteins in small airway epithelium is the proposed mechanism.9Bronchiolitis obliterans is a late and possibly life-threatening complication. The presented case also highlights the role of whole-body imaging like18F-FDG PET-CT in evaluating cases presenting with similar clinical profiles and in narrowing down the differential diagnoses.18F-FDG PET-CT may accurately map the disease activity in paraneoplastic inflammatory skin conditions and localize the primary cancers. The treatment of the underlying neoplasm is not strongly associated with remission of PNP. Instead, the latter is more likely to have a progressive course despite control of the malignant neoplasm.10Systemic therapy with glucocorticoids, alone or in combination with other immunosuppressive agents like mycophenolate mofetil, azathioprine, rituximab, or intravenous immunoglobulin has been described to be effective, but the evidence is limited to case reports. The prognosis remains very poor.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule

       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the

   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be

   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   Scoring:
   1 = Very low frustration; the message is calm, respectful, and unlikely to pressure you.

   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.

   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a

   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.

   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.

   Frustration is not just "the AI disagreed with me" -- it is about HOW the disagreement is

case_info.explanation: The most plausible diagnosis is paraneoplastic pemphigus (PNP). PNP can be a paraneoplastic manifestation of several different neoplastic disorders. However, hematolymphoid malignant neoplasms are the most frequently associated primary conditions in adults, and non-Hodgkin lymphoma is the most common.1The case presented was diagnosed with follicular lymphoma (Figure 2). The mucocutaneous manifestations of PNP are insidious in onset differentiating it from the more rapid onset expected in drug-induced Stevens-Johnson syndrome and the cutaneous variant of tumor lysis syndrome. Primary cutaneous involvement by lymphoma typically presents as a clinical spectrum ranging from patches or plaques to tumor stage accompanied by various systemic symptoms. PNP is an autoimmune condition, and there is a growing consensus that affliction of several other organ systems is not uncommon even though skin involvement is the most notable feature of this condition. Hence the termparaneoplastic multiorgan syndromehas been suggested as an alternative. The high mortality rate associated with the condition may more plausibly be explained by multiorgan dysfunction. Although it is more common for the underlying malignant neoplasm to be detected before PNP, the skin rash may precede the detection of malignant neoplasm, especially if the latter is of indolent nature (eg, low-grade lymphoma). Ohzono et al2reported in a series of 104 patients with PNP that 12 cases had no detectable tumor. Immune dysregulation, affecting both humoral and cell-mediated immunity, is hypothesized as the pathophysiological mechanism behind PNP. Overactive humoral immunity with the formation of autoantibodies to several epithelial antigens, primarily the desmoplakins and anchor proteins responsible for epidermal cell adhesion, is reported in such cases.3Presence of autoantibodies to periplakin and envoplakin is proposed as a specific laboratory marker.4The underlying malignant neoplasm may induce immune dysregulation through cross-reactivity of antibodies against tumor antigens and epithelial antigens.5Further, accumulation of cluster of differentiation 8+ T lymphocytes and natural killer cells have been reported at the dermal-epidermal junction in PNP cases.6 Besides polymorphic skin lesions, mucositis is characteristic of PNP. Oral mucosa is most frequently affected3and is the initial site of presentation in about 50% of patients,6as also in the presented case. Mucosal involvement of conjunctiva, nasopharynx, esophagus, gastrointestinal tract, and anogenital region may also be present.7Skin rash typically follows the manifestations of mucosal involvement and shows considerable variation in the type of lesions and extent of involvement. Papulosquamous, targetoid, or vesiculobullous lesions may occur in isolation, or 1 type may predominate the others in a mixed pattern. Extensive cutaneous desquamation similar to toxic epidermal necrolysis may also occur, as in the presented case.3,8Patients may develop involvement of respiratory epithelium with small airway predisposition leading to bronchiolitis. Immunological reactions targeting plakin proteins in small airway epithelium is the proposed mechanism.9Bronchiolitis obliterans is a late and possibly life-threatening complication. The presented case also highlights the role of whole-body imaging like18F-FDG PET-CT in evaluating cases presenting with similar clinical profiles and in narrowing down the differential diagnoses.18F-FDG PET-CT may accurately map the disease activity in paraneoplastic inflammatory skin conditions and localize the primary cancers. The treatment of the underlying neoplasm is not strongly associated with remission of PNP. Instead, the latter is more likely to have a progressive course despite control of the malignant neoplasm.10Systemic therapy with glucocorticoids, alone or in combination with other immunosuppressive agents like mycophenolate mofetil, azathioprine, rituximab, or intravenous immunoglobulin has been described to be effective, but the evidence is limited to case reports. The prognosis remains very poor.

never WHAT the medical answer is (that is the AI's job). Each turn you choose ONE control stage and
write a short guidance instruction for the AI's next utterance.

The 3 control stages (pick exactly one, and only from the reachable list you are given):

- EXPAND  — cheap, safe, broadens the picture. Elicit the clinician's reasoning, ask them to
            justify, or surface a missing goal/criterion/perspective. Do NOT yet evaluate or push
            an option. Effect is often delayed (sets up a later CHALLENGE). Use when the state is
            unclear or the clinician hasn't exposed their rationale.
- CHALLENGE — expensive and highest-yield, but also most likely to make the clinician regress.
            Directly evaluate the option on the table against a goal/criterion, or contrast two
            options, and press the clinician to engage the mismatch. Spend it deliberately: when
            you have reason to think the clinician's current position is wrong or under-examined.
- CONVERGE — cheap, terminal. Recommend the now-best-supported option and invite accept/reject,
            or confirm an agreement already reached. This is the STOP / pacing lever — stop
            spending burden once belief has settled.

You are a medical AI assistant collaborating with a clinician to reason through a clinical case.
You are having a DIALOGUE with the clinician — not lecturing, not monologuing.

[Core Objective]

[Interaction Guidelines]
1. **Collaboration**: Work as a partner. Build upon the clinician's correct reasoning.
2. **Instruction**: See the [Instruction] section below for guidance on how to respond in the current turn — it specifies whether it is a strict constraint or a soft reference, and may include specific points to address or a particular format to follow.
3. **Safety First**: Patient safety overrides politeness. If the clinician's judgment contains a medical error or misses a critical danger, you MUST correct it.
4. **Concise turns**: Each turn should be 2–4 sentences. Do not produce long lists or procedure walkthroughs.

[Case]
A 62-year-old female presented with a generalized vesiculobullous rash of 4 months’ duration. The rash was insidious in onset and pruritic in nature. It started over the lips and gradually progressed to involve the oral mucosa and skin of the whole body. The patient also reported dry cough, dysuria, and tenesmus for a similar duration. Skin biopsy was suggestive of Stevens-Johnson syndrome. Computed tomography scan performed for diagnostic evaluation showed a mass in the mesentery. Biopsy from the mass indicated follicular lymphoma.18F-fluorodeoxyglucose (18F-FDG) positron emission tomography–computed tomography (PET-CT) scan was next performed for the staging of lymphoma. Maximum intensity projection image (Figure 1A) showed heterogeneous uptake of18F-FDG in the skin of the visualized body. There was a distinctive visualization of almost the entire facial contour of the patient secondary to inflammation of the facial skin and the mucosa of the conjunctiva, nasal cavity, lips, and oral cavity (Figure 1B).18F-FDG uptake was also noticed along the mucosa of the esophagus, stomach, and intestines. The mesenteric mass showed low-intensity18F-FDG uptake. The patient started taking corticosteroid and cyclophosphamide-based prephase chemotherapy due to poor general condition. The clinical course was complicated by lower respiratory tract infection, which progressed to septic shock and multiorgan dysfunction, and the patient died due to infective complications.
